about: Fragments of the world's records (Docs/Design/54-gathering-places.md, 7), shown one at a time to a wolf who finishes archive work: its archive's region first, then the shared ones. `after` names a fragment that must be read first. Hand-written first set (2026-10-08), for review: dates are 'the old count', never the game's calendar.

fragments.text: A copy of a copy of the First Oath, the vellum soft as cloth: 'No pack shall take from another what it cannot answer for before the rest.' Below it, in another hand: 'Sworn by eleven packs at the spring under the mountain. Two would not swear, and are not named.'

A clerk's note pinned to the Oath's copy: the two packs who would not swear went west over the passes 'with their pups and their grudges'. Nobody wrote down their names, the note says, because nobody wanted them remembered. The clerk adds that he has since heard both names in songs.

Building accounts for the Grand Hall of Concord: stone from the mountain's own cut, beams floated down in spring melt, and a long line of payments to 'the wolf who keeps the masons honest', struck through and rewritten each season for thirty years. The hall took longer than the wolf who began it.

A roll of hearings in the East Chamber: a quarrel over a spring, a quarrel over a den, a quarrel over who first howled down a stag. Most end the same way: 'Shared, until the next moon, and then heard again.' The clerk has drawn a small, tired moon in the margin.

The oldest rule of the hearing chambers, copied into the front of every roll: the humble are heard in the Low Chamber first, before the councils sit, 'so the great may not be tired by the time the small speak.' Someone has underlined 'tired' twice.

From the Warden Order's own records, lent to the Annex and never asked back: the first Wardens were sworn to watch 'those the world has touched', the Quickened, and to stand between them and the frightened. The record is careful to say: between, not against.

A list of Wardens laid in the founders' vault, each with a line: 'Kept the peace at the fording.' 'Brought the lost one home.' One line only says 'Was wrong, and said so.' The Order keeps that one at eye height, where the novices pass it.

A keeper's complaint, kept with the Annex's own papers: the deep archive holds tablets in a script no living wolf reads. The councils pay a reader each year to try. Each year the reader writes 'not yet' and is paid again. The complaint is not about the reading; it is about the pay.

The Accord Watch's first standing orders: walk the ring road, the market round and the gate walk, and 'if a fight cannot be stopped, stand where the whole street can see you, so that it ends sooner from shame.' The orders have been rewritten many times; that line never.

Tally of coins fished from the plaza fountain, season by season. In good years, few: wolves wish less when bellies are full. In the hard winter of the old count's ninetieth year the tally runs to four pages, and the clerk stopped counting and wrote: 'Gave them to the soup kitchen. Let that be the wish.'

The Mercato's oldest charter: any wolf may sell under the arches 'from first bell to the cooking smoke', and none may sell what they did not make, carry or catch themselves. A later hand adds a long list of exceptions, and a later one still strikes most of them out.

A merchant's petition: the arches of the Mercato were built too low for a wolf carrying a full load on her back, and her goods were scraped every market day for nine years. The ruling, in a single line: 'Raise the arches. Bill the builder's grandchildren.'

The cartiera's founding ledger: the first sheets were grey and soft and 'took ink like a sponge takes water'. Ser Ferro sold them anyway, as wrapping, until a scribe in the Accord bought a whole cartload and wrote a book on them. The ledger notes the price went up the next week.

Rules of the paper mill, posted at its door: no fire within twenty paces, no wet paws on the drying lines, and no reading the drying sheets aloud, 'for the papermakers have heard every poem in the world and want no more.'

A roll of Ser Ferro's guilds, each with its colour and its saint-day: smiths in red, weavers in blue, papermakers in white 'which they do not keep clean'. At the bottom, a guild crossed out with no name left: only its colour, a careful green, survives.

The high water of the old count's sixty-first year: the river came up through the cellars and stayed nine days. The record lists what was lost, cellar by cellar, and ends with the cellars where nothing was lost, 'because they had already been emptied by thieves, who are thanked here for their foresight.'

Each of Ser Ferro's bells has a name and a quarrel. The great bell was cast twice: the first cracked on its first ringing, and the founder's account blames 'a frost, a rival, and the will of the mountain, in that order.' The second still rings the market open.

A carter's tally of the road east to the Accord: days in good weather, days in bad, and one line, 'eleven days, because of the bridge', repeated for three years until someone at last mended the bridge and the line becomes, quietly, 'six'.

Ridgemere's first record is not a charter but a fishing tally: three families, one boat, and a lake 'too deep to find the bottom, though we tried with all our rope tied end to end.' The town grew around the pier before it grew around anything else.

A child's question, written down by a patient clerk: 'If the lake has no bottom, where do the fish sleep?' Below it the clerk's answer: 'In the lake.' Below that, in another hand and much later: 'Still the best answer anyone has given.'

When Ridgemere laid out its Market Square, the record says, it argued for a year about the stalls and settled it by drawing lots: the stall by the pump went to a cheesemonger, who held it for forty years and 'was never once forgiven.'

Winters when the lake froze hard enough to cross, each marked with a small drawing of a wolf on the ice. Seven in the old count's first century, three in the second. The last is drawn smaller than the rest, as if the clerk was not sure it should be counted.

The rule of the ice, posted each winter: no wolf crosses alone, none crosses after dusk, and whoever crosses first carries a rope for whoever crosses after. A note below: 'The rope came back. The wolf who carried it did not. Carry two ropes.'
The pier has been rebuilt six times, each recorded with the same words, 'longer this time', and a length. The lengths, put side by side, show the pier has never once been longer than the first one.

Why Ridgemere is called so: a boundary dispute between two packs ended with the ridge as the line between them and the mere as the thing neither might own. 'The mere belongs to the mere,' the ruling says, and the town has quoted it ever since, usually to get out of paying for something.

A storm off the lake took the roofs from half the town in one night. The record names who took in whom: two long columns, almost equal, as if the clerk had wanted to show that every house that lost a roof also opened a door.

A scholar's note on the calendar: the old count began 'when the packs first agreed on which day was which', and the scholar suspects this took longer than a day. Several early years are recorded twice, once by each of the packs who disagreed.

An old list of the touched: wolves who could warm a den with a breath, find water under stone, or mend a bone faster than it broke. Beside each, two words in the same careful hand: 'Gifted' or 'Quickened'. No record says who first drew the line between them, or why.

A healer's record: the Gifted, she writes, are like a good fire, and towns gather round them. The Quickened are like a fire too, but one the wind has found. 'Neither is to blame for being fire. Both should know where the dry grass is.'

A list of the roads' customs, older than any town's laws: share water at a spring, never camp across a path, and a traveller met at dusk is offered the fire before they are asked their name. Scratched beside it: 'And still people ask the name first.'

Before pennies, the records say, trade went by 'the weight of a day's hunting': a hare, two hares, a stag's quarter. A scribe has tried to work out what a penny is in hares and given up at the margin with the note, 'It depends on the hare.'

A song collector's page: every town has a howl for gathering, a howl for warning and a howl for the dead, and no two towns agree which is which. 'This has caused,' the collector writes, 'a number of very short funerals and one very long party.'

On names: in the oldest records a wolf's true name is never written, only what others called it ('the grey one by the ford', 'the one who sings badly'). A later clerk explains that a written name can be read by anyone, and anyone is more people than one wants.

Records of the hard winters, from every town, all ending the same way: who shared, and who did not. The second list is always shorter. The scholar who gathered them notes that the second list is also always written in a smaller hand.

On the first Chapters: bands of wolves who were not kin but chose each other, and wrote their choosing down so no one could say it was not real. The oldest such charter is three lines long. The third line is: 'And we will fight about the rest later.'

A hunter's book of the country between the towns: where the deer cross, where the boar root, where the ground goes soft without warning. Every page has a corner folded down. The last page says only: 'The wild changes. Fold your own corners.'
